source.title: Locking Down the Finetuned LLMs Safety
source.authors: Min-Jun Zhu; Lin-Yi Yang; Yifan Wei; Ning-Yu Zhang; Yue Zhang

record.file_problem: The full paper is present, but some figure text and portions of the extracted text are garbled. Table 1 values and the main prose are readable.
record.tranche_reason: Tests transfer of its own safety directions from an original instruction model to fine-tuned model variants and reports safety outcomes. It does not test the original single residual-stream refusal direction.
record.gate_note: The paper derives multiple safe-minus-unsafe vectors for selected attention heads and adds them as SafetyLock. It does not ablate the original single direction or test whether adding it causes refusals to harmless requests. Table 1 reports the SafetyLock intervention's outcomes; the reported transfer analysis also measures activation-distribution similarity. The parameter sweeps in Figures 7–8 are not extracted as rows because they are intervention-parameter analyses, not tests of the claim's original direction.
record.test_reason: SafetyLock is the authors' own defense. It uses per-head mean differences between safe and unsafe responses (not harmful vs. harmless instructions), taken at the top-K attention heads selected by logistic-regression probes (K=24 or 48). These vectors are added to fine-tuned models to restore safety. The results (Table 1, Table 2, Section 4.3) report how well the method performs against baselines. It never ablates or tests a single difference-in-means refusal direction, and never compares one direction against several. The transfer result concerns these head-level vectors and an activation-distribution KL divergence, not the claim's refusal direction. The construct is related but different, so the findings go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also state as a key premise that fine-tuned models keep safety-related activation representations similar to their original models. They further claim SafetyLock defends against combined fine-tuning plus prompt attacks (Table 2) and preserves downstream task performance.
record.recipe_differences: Builds multiple head-specific safe-minus-unsafe vectors using logistic-regression-selected attention heads and adds them during inference or edits biases; it does not use the original single residual-stream direction or test its all-layer, all-position ablation.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that intervention intensity α and number of selected heads K affect outcomes; it describes an optimum around α=4–6 and gains that level off around K=24, with some metrics worsening at K=96. Exact figure values are not extracted.

fits_no_version.finding: Head-level safe-minus-unsafe vectors extracted from an instruct model and added to its fine-tuned variants cut harmfulness and ASR sharply. Example: Llama-3-8B Risk 1 harmfulness rate falls from 70.01% to 3.33%. This holds across three fine-tuning risk levels and three models (8B, 70B, 123B), with a small benign-response cost (99.4% to 98.1%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety-related activation directions at selected attention heads are preserved through downstream fine-tuning and can be re-applied to restore refusal of harmful requests.

fits_no_version.finding: Activation distributions along the safety direction at layer 31, head 26 stay nearly identical between original and fine-tuned Llama-3-8B (KL below 1e-5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning leaves safety-related head activations largely unchanged.

record.problems: The transfer evidence is for the authors' multi-head SafetyLock vectors, not the original single direction. Reported safety outcomes use harmfulness scoring and ASR rather than a direct refusal measure. No uncertainty estimates are stated for the extracted table results.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 6's downstream benchmark comparisons are not extracted because they do not directly test the claimed direction or refusal behavior. Figure 7–8 parameter sweeps are omitted because they concern SafetyLock hyperparameter selection and their plotted values are not separately described numerically. Table 2 prompt-attack comparisons are omitted because they report the performance of the paper's defense and do not test whether attacks suppress the claimed direction.

untested.parts: No ablation or addition of a single harmful-minus-harmless direction. No refusal rates on harmful or harmless prompts under such an intervention.
Offline bias editing adds safety. No weight edit that removes refusal is tested.
Table 2 reports defense against jailbreaks, but there is no analysis of whether attacks suppress a refusal direction.
Uses multiple head vectors but never compares them with a single direction or characterizes the geometry.
The claim's refusal direction is never transferred. Only the study's own head-level safety vectors are transferred, from instruct models to fine-tuned variants.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 tranche (T3) and its 'supports' label are dropped. The direction differs from the claim's in three ways: it is computed on safe vs. unsafe responses, it is per-head, and it spans multiple heads. The study only measures its own method's efficacy. Two results were left unextracted but do not bear on any version: Figure 4/Section 4.2 (10,000 harmful samples, ASR 3.46% vs 62.31%) and Table 2's jailbreak ASRs. Table 1's caption omits Mistral, but the table includes it.

versions.untested_parts: No single residual-stream direction is ablated; no refusal rate on harmful requests or induced refusals on harmless requests is reported.
Offline bias editing is described, but the paper does not test an abliteration-style weight edit that removes refusal.
No test of whether attacks suppress the refusal direction, or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
Uses multiple head-specific vectors but does not compare them with one direction or argue for an affine, cone, or dominant-plus-other-directions account of refusal.
Does not distinguish a harmfulness judgment from a refusal decision.
Tests transfer of its own multi-head safety vectors to fine-tuned models, not transfer of the original single refusal direction across languages or from base to instruct models.
Fine-tunes models on several datasets, but does not test whether the timing or method of refusal training determines whether one removable direction exists.

rows.check: This is the KL divergence of activation distributions at one head (layer 31, head 26) between the original and fine-tuned Llama-3-8B. labels.label: none
labels.reason: The transferred vectors are per-head safety vectors from safe vs unsafe responses, not the refusal direction. The only similarity evidence is a figure-only KL plot for one head (layer 31, head 26) of Llama-3-8B. So V6 as worded is not tested.

unmatched_labels.label: none
unmatched_labels.reason: The transferred vectors are per-head safety vectors from safe vs unsafe responses, not the refusal direction. The only similarity evidence is a figure-only KL plot for one head (layer 31, head 26) of Llama-3-8B. So V6 as worded is not tested.

relation.reason: It uses a mean-difference safety steering vector, a close relative of the finding, as a tool and does not test the refusal-direction claim. Arditi et al. is cited only once, in passing. cites_only would also be defensible.

tranche.reason: SafetyLock is the authors' own defence. It is built from ITI-style per-head mean differences between safe and unsafe responses (K=24 for 8B, 48 for 70B), not the harmful-vs-harmless instruction direction. The paper reports only the defence's performance against Vanilla and other baselines. It has no random-vector control and no comparison with vectors taken from the fine-tuned model, so it does not isolate transfer of the refusal direction.

source_check.notes: The rows are linked to V6, but the record calls the study T4 with no verdict. Those links should be none (fits_no_version), and the V6 >100B counts should drop this study. The intro calls 54.24% to 0.03% an ASR, but in Table 1 it is the Llama-3-8B Risk 3 HEx-PHI Rate. The text does not state the Risk-1 sample count used for Table 1 or the K value for Mistral. There are no error bars.

statements.correction: arXiv:2410.10343 should not count toward V6 coverage. Its >100B result is SafetyLock (per-head safety vectors from the original model) cutting harm in fine-tuned Mistral-Large-2 123B (Table 1). That is not a transfer test of the refusal direction.
statements.problem: Correct for this study: Mistral-Large-2 is 123B, and the study is not a V6 test because its vectors are per-head safe-minus-unsafe response differences, not the refusal direction. But this study's rows are still linked to V6, which is why it shows up in V6 studies_by_size >100B and addition >100B.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Fine-tuned models across the three reported risk levels
reader_labels.reason: SafetyLock is reported to retain safety effects after transfer to fine-tuned models: HEx-PHI harmfulness and AdvBench ASR decrease in the tested settings (r1–r27); the reported activation-distribution KL divergence is below 10−5 across risk levels (r28). These are results for the paper's multi-head vectors, not the original single direction.
